title: Octavius
author: Marcus Minucius Felix

passages.original: Quid? Mantuanus Maro nonne apertius, proximius, verius principio ait caelum ac terras et cetera mundi membra spiritus intus alit et infusa mens agitat, inde hominum pecudumque genus et quicquid aliud animalium? Idem alio loco mentem istam et spiritum deum nominat.
passages.english: What? Does not Maro of Mantua say more openly, more closely, more truly: "In the beginning a spirit within nourishes the sky and the lands and the other members of the world, and a mind poured through [them] sets [them] in motion; from this [come] the race of men and of beasts," and whatever other living creatures [there are]? The same [poet] in another place names that mind and spirit god.
passages.notes: Maro of Mantua is Virgil; the quotation paraphrases Aeneid 6.724–728. The poet's lines are embedded in Minucius' prose and given here as prose.

passages.original: Omitto illos rudes et veteres, qui de suis dictis sapientes esse meruerunt. Sit Thales Milesius omnium primus, qui primus omnium de caelestibus disputavit. Is autem Milesius Thales rerum initium aquam dixit, deum autem eam mentem quae ex aqua cuneta formaverit. Esto altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inveniri, a deo traditum: vides philosophi principalis nobiscum penitus opinionem consonare.
passages.english: I pass over those rough and ancient men who earned the name of wise for their sayings. Let Thales of Miletus be first of all, who first of all disputed about heavenly things. This Thales of Miletus said that the beginning of things was water, and that god was that mind which formed all things out of water. Granted that the account of water and spirit is too lofty and sublime to have been discovered by a man, [and was] handed down by god: you see that the opinion of the foremost philosopher agrees entirely with ours.
passages.notes: 'cuneta' is a scanning error for 'cuncta'. The construction 'Esto ... a deo traditum' is compressed; translated as a concession.

passages.original: Eadem fere Chrysippus: vim divinam rationalem, naturam et mundum, interim et fatalem necessitatem deum credit Zenonemque interpretatione physiologica in Hesiodi, Homeri Orpheique carminibus imitatur.
passages.english: Chrysippus [says] almost the same: he believes that god is a rational divine force, nature and the world, and at times fatal necessity; and he imitates Zeno in a physical interpretation of the poems of Hesiod, Homer and Orpheus.
passages.notes: 'fatalem necessitatem' means the necessity of fate. 'interpretatione physiologica' refers to allegorical interpretation in terms of natural philosophy.

passages.original: Loquitur Plato partes orbis nunc inundare nunc alternis vicibus ardescere, et cum ipsum mundum perpetuum et insolubilem diceret esse fabricatum, addit tamen, ipsi artifici deo soli et solubilem et esse mortalem.
passages.english: Plato says that parts of the world now are flooded, now in alternating turns burst into flame; and although he said that the world itself was built everlasting and indissoluble, he nevertheless adds that to the craftsman god himself alone it is both dissoluble and mortal.
passages.notes: The sense of the last clause is that only the god who made it can dissolve it.
